newsitem.title: EGYPT: Palestinians blast Israel at Cairo conference.
newsitem.headline: Palestinians blast Israel at Cairo conference.

text.p: Palestinians lashed out at Israel at a Middle East economic conference on Tuesday, accusing its right-wing government of strangling their economy and hindering regional cooperation.

"We have been unable to do any substantial business with the rest of the world and also with our neighbours Jordan and Egypt," said Maher Masri, Palestinian economy and trade minister, referring to Israeli closures of self-rule areas.
"We cannot survive under such circumstances...poverty never produces peace," he said.
The third annual Middle East and North Africa economic conference got down to the business of doing business in the volatile region after a flurry of diplomatic activity earlier in the day.

U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher, who met Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak and Palestinian President Yasser Arafat on the sidelines of the conference, said he believed an Israel-PLO agreement on Hebron was "close at hand".
But Christopher's spokesman Nicholas Burns advised journalists against expecting a deal in the next few days on implementing a long overdue Israeli troop redeployment from the West Bank town.
Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy came to the conference for the day to meet Christopher but did not address the meeting, which he appeared to criticise in remarks to reporters. "This

conference which is taking place in Cairo is different from the previous conferences...which had a political dimension and which included Israel in the preparations and the substance," he said. "This conference is an Egyptian economic conference."
In the plenary and at specialist sessions on economic issues at the conference, Palestinians went on the offensive.

"Regional development projects just cannot be achieved until there is an achievement on the political front -- until there is a just and balanced peace," said Palestinian Finance Minister Zuhdi al-Nashashibi.
"The party that is snagging the peace process and stalling on implementing the peace pledges it has signed is totally responsible for hindering regional cooperation," he said, referring to Israel.

The West Bank and Gaza have been subject to periodic closures since 1993, the year Israel and the PLO signed landmark peace deals. A blanket closure Israel imposed on the areas after a wave of Islamist suicide attacks killed 59 in February and March has only recently been eased.

The closures, which bar Arab workers from reaching jobs in Israel and prevent manufacturers from exporting goods and importing raw materials, have plunged an already badly battered economy into deep depression.
Palestinian real national income (GNP) has dropped by 23 percent since 1992, according to the U.N. Special Coordinator in the Occupied Territories.
David Brodet, director general of Israel's finance ministry, said during a panel discussion with Masri that Israel had no choice but to impose tight security restrictions after the suicide bombings.
Israel, he said, simply wanted to ensure that its "children can go to school every morning without any damage".
